title: Non-communicable diseases
examples: What are some things that increase my risk of getting heart disease?
If two things happen together, does it mean one causes the other?
How can I tell if a study shows a link or a cause?

explain.say: Today we are learning about non-communicable diseases.
First we will look at risk factors for these diseases.
A risk factor increases your chance of getting a disease.
Next we must understand correlation versus causation.
For example, we might see ice cream sales and sunburns together.
In real life, if people who exercise more have lower blood pressure.

faq.q: What is the difference between correlation and causation?
faq.a: Correlation means two things are linked or happen together. Causation means one thing directly causes the other to happen.
asks: Does linking two things mean one causes the other?
What is the difference between association and cause?

faq.q: Are risk factors the same as causes?
faq.a: No, a risk factor increases your chance, but it might not be the sole cause. Lifestyle choices are key risk factors.
asks: If I have a risk factor, will I definitely get the disease?
Can I prevent a disease just by changing my risk factors?

faq.a: Scientists often use controlled studies where they change one thing and measure the effect on another thing.
asks: Do they need experiments to prove it?
What kind of study shows cause?

faq.q: What are some major non-communicable diseases?
faq.a: Major examples include heart disease, certain types of cancer, and type two diabetes. These are often linked to lifestyle.
asks: What are the big diseases we should worry about?
Are these diseases always caused by bad habits?

faq.q: Can changing my diet reduce my risk?
faq.a: Yes, making healthier choices in your diet can significantly lower your risk for many chronic diseases.
asks: Is diet the most important thing for health?
How much does diet affect my future health?

facts: Non-communicable diseases are not spread from person to person.
Risk factors are things that increase the probability of developing a disease.
Correlation means a relationship exists between two variables.
Causation means one variable directly produces a change in another.

quiz.say: If a study shows that people who eat red meat often have higher cholesterol, this shows:
quiz.why: It only shows a link, not that red meat causes high cholesterol.

wrong.0: This is an action, not a description of the relationship found.
wrong.2: This is wrong because the study might be missing other factors.
wrong.3: This is too general; it describes the finding, not the relationship type.

quiz.say: A person who never exercises and smokes has a higher risk of heart disease because:
quiz.why: Having several risk factors together increases the overall danger.

wrong.0: The risk factor itself is not the disease; it increases the chance.
wrong.1: This ignores the impact of lack of exercise.
wrong.2: This is too absolute; lifestyle changes can still help.

quiz.say: If we see that students who study more for exams also get better grades, we can say:
quiz.why: They are related, but we need more proof to say studying causes the grade.

wrong.0: There is clearly a positive relationship shown by the data.
wrong.2: While studying helps, other factors like sleep also play a role.
wrong.3: This ignores the importance of things like diet and rest.
